'''Abdul Hameed Nayyar''' (Born 1945), also known as '''A.H. Nayyar''', is a [[Pakistan|Pakistani]] [[physicist]], author, and freelance [[Political consulting|consultant]] on the issues of [[Education in Pakistan|education]], [[Nuclear safety and security|nuclear safety]], and [[Renewable energy|energy]].<ref name="Eqbal Ahmad Centre for Public Education">{{cite web |title=A.H. Nayyar {{!}} Eqbal Ahmad Centre for Public Education |url=http://eacpe.org/about-a-h-nayyar/ |website=www.eacpe.org |accessdate=29 April 2020}}</ref> His field of specialization is the physics of [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter]], and he has served in the faculties of the [[Quaid-e-Azam University]] in [[Islamabad]] from 1973 till 2005 and the [[Lahore University of Management Sciences]].<ref name="Eqbal Ahmad Centre for Public Education"/> Nayyar is known for calling for [[Education in Pakistan|education reforms]] and military [[Nuclear arms control|arms control]], about which he directed research programs at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute in [[Islamabad]].<ref name="American Physical Society"/> He is also one of the founding members of [[The Black Hole (community center)|The Black Hole]], an intellectual space in Islamabad, Pakistan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Black Hole – Science – Art – Culture |url=https://theblackhole.pk/ |access-date=2024-01-29 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Biography==

Nayyar was born in [[Hyderabad]], [[British India]], in 1945, to a  [[Punjabi Muslim]] [[Khatri]] family. His family moved to Pakistan after [[Partition of India]] 1947.<ref name="International Centre for Theoretical Physics">{{cite book |last1=Physics |first1=International Centre for Theoretical |title=Directory of physicists from developing countries |date=1987 |publisher=International Centre for Theoretical Physics |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K5TvAAAAMAAJ&q=nayyar+physics+born+1945 |accessdate=29 April 2020 |language=en}}</ref> He was educated in [[Karachi]], and attended the [[University of Karachi|Karachi University]] where he graduated with [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] in [[Physics]] in 1964, and [[Master of Science|MSc]] in Physics from Karachi University in 1966.<ref name="American Physical Society">{{cite web |title=2018 Stanley Corrsin Award Recipient |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Nayyar&first_nm=Abdul&year=2010 |website=www.aps.org |publisher=American Physical Society |accessdate=29 April 2020 |language=en}}</ref>{{rp|269}}<ref name="Zed Books">{{cite book |last1=Khan |first1=Mohammad Asghar |title=Islam, politics, and the state: the Pakistan experience |date=1985 |publisher=Zed Books |isbn=978-0-86232-471-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T9AlAQAAMAAJ&q=abdul%20hameed%20nayyar%20 |accessdate=29 April 2020 |language=en}}</ref> 

Nayyar went to [[United Kingdom]] for his doctoral studies, attending the [[Imperial College, London|Imperial College]] in [[London]] where he obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in [[condensed matter physics]] in 1973.<ref name="American Physical Society" /> His thesis covered studies on [[magnetic properties]] of the [[Electron excitation|excited electrons]].<ref name="International Centre for Theoretical Physics"/> Upon returning to Pakistan, he joined the [[Institute of Theoretical Physics, Qau|Institute of Theoretical Physics]] (now department of physics) of the [[Quaid-i-Azam University]] (QaU) and served on the faculty until 2005.<ref name="American Physical Society" /> 

After leaving [[Quaid-i-Azam University|QaU]] in 2005, Nayyar became involved with the public policy issues regarding the [[Education in Pakistan|education]], [[Renewable energy|renewable]] and [[FuelCell Energy|fuel cell]] [[Energy (physics)|energy]] at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) in Islamabad.<ref name="princeton">{{cite web |title=Abdul H. Nayyar {{!}} Princeton Science & Global Security |url=https://sgs.princeton.edu/team/abdul-h-nayyar |website=sgs.princeton.edu |publisher=princeton university |accessdate=30 April 2020}}</ref> Since 1998, Nayyar has been a visiting research scholar at the [[Princeton University]] in the [[United States]], and has been on the faculty to instruct courses on physics at the [[Lahore University of Management Sciences]] in [[Pakistan]].<ref name="princeton"/>

==Political advocacy==
===Education, peace, and energy===

Dr. Nayyar co-edited the SDPI report "The Subtle Subversion: The State of Curricula and Textbooks in Pakistan",<ref>http://www.sdpi.org SDPI</ref><ref name="subtle">Nayyar, A.H. and Salim, A. (eds.)(2003). [https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20090205032614/http://www.sdpi.org/whats_new/reporton/State%20of%20Curr&TextBooks.pdf The subtle Subversion: A report on Curricula and Textbooks in Pakistan]. Report of the project ''A Civil Society Initiative in Curricula and Textbooks Reform''. Sustainable Development Policy Institute, Islamabad.</ref> published in 2003, the report critically examined curriculum guidelines and textbook contents in the mainstream public school system of Pakistan. The report, which was intensely debated on public forums, eventually led to the government exercise to revise school curricula and textbooks (see: [[Pakistan Studies curriculum]]).<ref>Ghauri, I. (2006). ''[http://www.dailytimes.com.pk/default.asp?page=2006\12\07\story_7-12-2006_pg1_1 School curriculum ‘enlightened’; Two-Nation Theory explained]''. [[Daily Times (Pakistan)|Daily Times]]. 7 December. Retrieved on 5 June 2008</ref> Also from SDPI, he co-authored a critical appraisal of the [[National Education Policy]], published in 2006. He has also researched and written on Madrassa education. For over a year, he served as the Executive Director of Developments in Literacy, an organisation of [[Pakistani Americans]] for philanthropic intervention in education to disadvantaged communities in Pakistan. Also for a year in 2010, he served as the Director of the Ali Institute of Education, Lahore. He has since authored a number of articles further criticising the state of education in Pakistan.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1243391|title=Science education in schools|last=Nayyar|first=A. H.|date=2016-03-04|website=DAWN.COM|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1182401|title=War to mould minds|last=Nayyar|first=A. H.|date=2015-05-17|website=DAWN.COM|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>

===Peace activism===

Dr. Nayyar also takes an active interest in the national and international peace movements. Dr. Nayyar is a member of the Global Council of Abolition 2000.

===Anti-nuclear movement===

Another area that interests him is [[nuclear disarmament]]. He holds a visiting position at the Program on Science and Global Security of the [[Woodrow Wilson School]] at [[Princeton University]], US, where he spends summer months conducting technical studies on issues in nuclear disarmament. He is a member of the [[International Panel on Fissile Materials]].

===Renewable energy===

In the area of [[renewable energy]], the energy group at SDPI that he helped establish, has studied the question of marketability of renewable energy technologies with a view to identifying policy measures that could promote their use in Pakistan.
